text: Fidelity is faithfulness to the original — how exactly a copy, description, or reproduction matches the real thing. A map with perfect fidelity would reproduce the landscape detail for detail, which is exactly why it would stop being useful: it would no longer simplify anything. The word can also mean loyalty to a person or promise; both senses share the idea of staying true.

Dogma is belief treated as unquestionably true — accepted on authority and never re-checked against evidence. The article warns against using maps as dogma: a model you refuse to question keeps steering you long after the world it described has changed.

To distill something is to boil it down to its essential core. Literally it means purifying a liquid by heating and condensing it; figuratively — as with financial statements distilling thousands of transactions into a few numbers — it means extracting just the important part from a mass of detail.

Here a reduction is a simplified version — something with most of the detail deliberately stripped out, not a price cut. Maps are reductions of the territory: that loss of detail is what makes them usable at all.
A snapshot is a picture of one single moment — so calling a map a snapshot means it shows the world as it was when the map was made, with no promise that the world still looks like that now.

Anecdotes are individual stories or firsthand reports — 'a customer told me they waited forever' — as opposed to systematic data. Bezos's rule that when the data and the anecdotes disagree, the anecdotes are usually right, flips the usual advice: a vivid story can be the early warning that your measurements are broken.

A metric is a number a company tracks to measure how something is going — wait time, sales, clicks. Metrics are maps of performance: useful summaries that can quietly stop matching what customers actually experience.

An abstraction is a general, simplified idea pulled away from messy specifics — 'the economy' instead of millions of individual purchases. Maps and models are abstractions: handy compressions of reality, dangerous only when you forget the compression happened.
Static here means fixed and unchanging — not TV fuzz. Static rules keep enforcing yesterday's map on today's world, which is the article's warning against locking a model in place.
Dynamic is the opposite of static: constantly moving and changing. Saying the world is dynamic is the reason maps go stale — the territory keeps shifting after the map is drawn.
Celestial means belonging to the sky or outer space — celestial motion is the movement of planets, moons, and stars. Newton's physics mapped that motion so well it guided astronomy for centuries.

To delimit something is to mark exactly where its boundaries are. Physicists delimit Newton's and Einstein's theories — they know, to many decimal places, where each one works and where it stops — which is precisely the skill of knowing your map's limits.

Uncharted literally means not yet mapped — no chart exists for it. Uncharted territory is any area, like quantum mechanics in the article, where your existing maps simply don't apply and you have to explore carefully.

A cartographer is a person who makes maps. 'Consider the cartographer' means: every map reflects its maker's goals, values, and blind spots — so before trusting a map (or a news source, or a study), ask who made it and why.

Objective means based purely on facts, uninfluenced by anyone's opinions or interests. The article's point is that maps are not purely objective — choices about what to include and leave out always carry the mapmaker's perspective.
To depict something is to show or represent it, in a picture or a description. What a map depicts is what its maker chose to show — which is never everything.

To chronicle something is to record events carefully over time, like a historian. Jane Jacobs chronicled what city planners did to real neighborhoods — she documented it case by case, which is what made her critique so hard to dismiss.

As an adjective, elaborate means highly detailed and complicated. The planners' elaborate models looked impressive on paper — the article's point is that complexity in the model is no guarantee it matches how cities actually work.

To correspond to something is to match or line up with it. Cities were changed to correspond to the planners' models — reality was forced to fit the map, instead of the map being corrected to fit reality.
Reconciling two things means making them agree. Updating your map is a process of reconciling what you want to be true with what is true — and the wanting side usually puts up a fight.

A pundit is someone who gives opinions publicly as an expert — the commentators on news shows and podcasts. The article groups them with experts and teachers as people whose maps we borrow, which is why it matters to choose rigorous ones.
Rigorous means thorough, careful, and strict about standards — checking the work instead of hand-waving. A rigorous mapmaker tests their claims against reality before publishing them.
Here transparent means open about how you work — showing your sources, methods, and reasoning — not see-through like glass. A transparent expert lets you inspect how the map was drawn.

Terrain is the physical character of a stretch of land — its hills, rivers, and obstacles. The article uses it interchangeably with territory: the real ground you must deal with, whatever the map claims.
Predictive means able to tell you what will happen next. A model earns its keep by being explanatory and predictive — if it can't forecast anything about the territory, it's decoration, not a map.
Reliant on something means depending on it. We're reliant on maps other people made — teachers, experts, journalists — because nobody can explore every territory firsthand.

A résumé is the one-page summary of your education, jobs, and achievements that you send when applying for work. It's a perfect example of a map: a person with an outstanding résumé who can't do the job is a territory that doesn't match its map.
Solely means only, and nothing else. Relying solely on maps means trusting the summary alone and never checking reality — which is how the map's errors become your errors.
In line with something means matching or consistent with it. A wait-time metric in line with expectations means the number looked normal — which is exactly why nobody questioned it.

Waiting on hold means staying on a phone call, usually listening to music, until someone is available to help you. Bezos waited on hold for over ten minutes — the real customer experience his dashboard said couldn't happen.
On the flip side introduces the other side of the same situation — like flipping a coin or a record over. Newton's map still works; on the flip side, Einstein's isn't complete either.
To take something into account is to include it in your thinking before deciding. The article says to take into account three principles whenever you use a map or model.
A cautionary tale is a story told as a warning — here's what went wrong, don't repeat it. Jacobs's book is a cautionary tale about forcing real cities to fit tidy models.

To check all the boxes is to meet every listed requirement, like ticking items on a checklist. Someone who checks all the boxes on paper looks perfect by the map — the article's warning is that paper and performance are different things.

The physics of Isaac Newton (1600s–1700s): laws of motion and gravity that predict how objects move, from falling apples to orbiting planets. Still accurate enough for everyday engineering — it just breaks down at extreme speeds and scales.

Albert Einstein's 1905 theory showing that time and space aren't fixed — they stretch and shrink depending on how fast you're moving. It replaced Newton's map for things moving near the speed of light.

The physics of the very small — atoms and particles — where matter behaves in strange, probabilistic ways. Physicists still can't fully connect it to Einstein's physics, which is why the article calls it uncharted territory.

A feedback loop is when the results of your actions flow back to you as information that shapes what you do next — like feeling a bike tip and correcting. Close off the loop and errors pile up unseen; it's how maps, habits, and skills all go stale.

An American writer (1916–2006) whose book The Death and Life of Great American Cities took down the top-down city planning of her era. She showed that planners' neat models ignored how real streets and neighborhoods actually work.

A toll-free phone number in the US — calls cost the caller nothing because the company pays. Companies use them for customer service, which is why Bezos dialed one to test his own company's wait times.
A master plan is a single big blueprint meant to direct how an entire city or project develops for decades. Jacobs's warning: a master plan drawn for the statistical city can flatten the real one.
The standard summary reports of a company's money — what it earned, spent, owns, and owes. They distill thousands of transactions into a few pages: a map of the business, not the business itself.
